extracted.intended_audience: Users of the Magma computational algebra system (mathematicians and programmers doing algebra/number theory computations)
extracted.subtask_description: Reference/manual excerpt describing ring- and integer-related properties, intrinsics and recommended usage in the Magma computer algebra system, including definitions (unitary, finite, Euclidean, UFD), arithmetic, factorization, modular arithmetic, and residue class ring operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unitary ring / IsUnitary(R)
rubrics_metrics.description: An important ring property is whether it is unitary, that is, whether it has a multiplicative identity. This is tested by IsUnitary(R). Many Magma operations involving rings are only permitted if the ring is unitary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A subtlety: a subring is regarded as unitary by Magma only if it contains the multiplicative identity of its generic ring. Example: an ideal I of ZZ/30ZZ generated by 5 may have an element 25 acting as a multiplicative identity internally, but since I does not contain the 1 of ZZ/30ZZ it is not regarded as unitary by Magma (IsUnitary(I) returns false).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite ring / IsFinite(R)
rubrics_metrics.description: IsFinite(R) returns true if Magma knows that the ring R is finite. If true, the cardinality #R is also returned or can be obtained via #R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Magma knows the ring is finite, it can usually compute the elements (Set(R)) and allow iteration over R (e.g., use 'x in R' in constructors or for-loops). If not known finite, many element-level operations may be undefined or not computable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totally ordered ring / IsOrdered(R) and comparison intrinsics
rubrics_metrics.description: For elements of a totally ordered ring R, Magma provides comparison intrinsics x lt y, x le y, x gt y, x ge y and functions Maximum/Minimum, Max/Min, which operate sensibly only when a total ordering is defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a ring does not have a total ordering defined, comparing elements for size makes no sense. Integer ring, rational field and real field are examples of totally ordered rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclidean ring / IsEuclideanRing(R) and EuclideanNorm
rubrics_metrics.description: A Euclidean ring R is a ring which has a known Euclidean norm function φ from the set S of regular elements of R to the non-negative integers such that (a) x|y implies φ(x) ≤ φ(y) and (b) if x ∈ R and y ∈ S then there exist q, r ∈ R with x = yq + r and either r = 0 or φ(r) < φ(y). IsEuclideanRing(R) returns true if R is known to have a Euclidean norm; EuclideanNorm(x) returns φ(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common examples: integers (φ = absolute value) and univariate polynomials over a field (φ = degree). Purpose: allow division-with-remainder. Magma's knowledge of norms is restricted and uses standard mathematical choices. Quotrem(x,y) returns quotient and remainder; x mod y returns remainder; x div y returns quotient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclidean domain test / IsEuclideanDomain(R)
rubrics_metrics.description: IsEuclideanDomain(R) tests whether a Euclidean ring is also an integral domain (i.e., commonly-investigated Euclidean rings are integral domains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when algorithms require both Euclidean property and domain property; Magma has distinct intrinsics for these related properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique Factorization Domain (UFD) / IsUFD(R)
rubrics_metrics.description: A unique factorization domain (UFD) is a domain R such that every non-zero element factorizes uniquely (up to order and associates) into a product of irreducibles. IsUFD(R) returns true if R is known by Magma to be a UFD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operations provided for UFDs include GCD, LCM, XGCD, Factorization(x) which returns [<fi,ki>] and a unit u with x = u * product fi^ki. Also IsDivisible and IsAssociate. Example: Factorization(-3798386541) returns prime factors and unit -1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorization(x) and Factorization parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Factorization(x) returns the factorization of x (integers or polynomials) in the form of a factorization sequence and a unit. For polynomials the Factorization(f) intrinsic accepts parameters (e.g., Al) to choose algorithms; for integers Factorization(n) uses combinations of algorithms and accepts parameters like PollardRhoLimit and MPQSLimit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To specify desired method for polynomials, use Factorization(f: Al := "AlgorithmName"). Example: Al := "BerlekampSmall". For integers parameters can change algorithm mix/limits — the text warns 'these changes are not necessarily for the better!'. See later sections (e.g., 20.4.2) for parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integer and rational constructors and coercion rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Integer ring ZZ and rational field Q are automatically defined in Magma. Integers and rationals may be created by syntax (e.g., 42; 5/7;). IntegerRing() / Integers() return ZZ; RationalField() / Rationals() return Q. Magma distinguishes between integer  p and rational p/1 but automatic coercion makes this transparent; IsIntegral(r) returns true for rationals with denominator 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying strictly integer functions to rational arguments you may need explicit coercion (Integers() ! (374/2)) or use integer division 'div' to avoid type errors. Use elt< Q | p, q > or Q ! t for explicit rational constructors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic operator semantics (+, -, *, /, div, mod, Quotrem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard arithmetic operators available: +, -, *, /. Division operator / constructs rational a/b and always returns an element of the rational field; div returns integral quotient when applied to two integers; Quotrem(a,n) returns quotient q and remainder r with a = qn + r and |r| < |n|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mixing integers and rationals, results follow field/category rules (e.g., integer op rational → rational). Use Quotrem, div and mod appropriately to get integer quotient/remainder behavior. Example: Quotrem(123871,4249) returns q=29, r=650.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exponentiation and power semantics (m^k)
rubrics_metrics.description: m^k denotes k-th power of m. If exponent k is rational or real the result is real, but in chapter k assumed integer. Provided k is a non-negative integer and m integer, result is integer; otherwise often rational. By convention 0^0 is defined to be 1. The exponent k must be a small integer in Magma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parent() shows where result lives (Integer Ring vs Rational Field). Example: 3^5 -> 243 (Integer Ring); 3^(-5) -> 1/243 (Rational Field).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisibility and gcd/lcm intrinsics (GCD, LCM, XGCD, IsDivisible, IsEven/IsOdd)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotrem(a,n), a div n, a mod n, GCD(a,b), GCD(Q), XGCD(a,b) (returns d,p,q with d=pa+qb), LCM(a,b), LCM(Q), IsDivisible(a,b) (returns true and quotient if divisible), IsEven(a), IsOdd(a) are provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GCD and LCM have sequence variants. XGCD returns cofactors for expressing gcd as linear combination (use multiple assignment). Use these intrinsics in number-theoretic algorithms (examples show factoring by gcd of 2^m-1 with n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary integer/rational functions (Abs, Sign, Max, Min, Ilog2, Isqrt, Iroot, Intseq, Seqint, RandomBits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions Abs, Sign, Max, Min apply to integers and rationals (where meaningful). Ilog2 returns integer floor of base-2 log, Isqrt floor square root, Iroot floor n-th root. Intseq(a,b) returns base-b digit sequence; Seqint converts sequence back to integer. Random and RandomBits produce random integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Intseq(101,3) -> [2,0,2,0,1]. Use SafeSqrt example to show type-checking and error handling in user functions. Max/Min can take sequences and return position information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational-specific intrinsics (Numerator, Denominator, IsIntegral, Floor, Ceiling, Round, Truncate, RationalReconstruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerator(r), Denominator(r), IsIntegral(r) (true if denominator is one), Floor(r), Ceiling(r), Round(r) (n+1/2 rounds to n+1), Truncate(r) (round toward zero). RationalReconstruction(s) applied to s in ZZ/mZZ or GF(m) returns boolean and rational r if there exists unique r = p/q with |p|, q ≤ m/2 and residue s = p * q^-1 mod m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RationalReconstruction is useful as a partial inverse of reduction modulo m. Example: RationalReconstruction(GF(29)!20) -> true 2/3. It returns false if no such reconstruction exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetical multiplicative functions (EulerPhi, CarmichaelLambda, MoebiusMu, DivisorSigma, LegendreSymbol, JacobiSymbol)
rubrics_metrics.description: Magma provides standard multiplicative arithmetic functions: EulerPhi(n) (φ(n)), CarmichaelLambda(n) (λ(n)), MoebiusMu(n) (µ(n)), DivisorSigma(i,n) (σi(n)), LegendreSymbol(n,m) for odd prime m, JacobiSymbol(n,m) for odd m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most of these functions require prime factorization of n and hence are slow for large inputs; versions that accept a factorization sequence are provided. Legendre and Jacobi symbols are fast as they use reciprocity laws without factorization. Examples and formulas given (e.g., EulerPhi via product over prime powers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primality and factorization intrinsics (IsPrime, IsProbablyPrime, Factorization)
rubrics_metrics.description: IsPrime(n) returns true iff |n| is prime; may be slow for hundreds of digits. IsProbablyPrime is a faster probabilistic test (see later). Factorization(n) returns prime decomposition of |n| as a factorization sequence and ±1 for sign; each prime is subjected to primality proving algorithm used by IsPrime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factorization for moderate integers suffices for many tasks; for very large integers use parameter-tunable algorithms in later sections. Example: Factorization(123456789012345678901) returns listed primes and exponents; IsPrime applied to elements of factorization verifies primality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorization sequences (RngIntEltFact) and operations on them
rubrics_metrics.description: Factorization sequences are a special category (RngIntEltFact) allowing their use as inputs to functions to avoid recomputing factorization. They print like sequences of tuples [<p,k>, ...].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can multiply, divide (exact quotient required), add, subtract, and exponentiate factorization sequences directly. Use SeqFact to build a factorization sequence and Facint (FactorizationToInteger) to convert back to integer. Errors if sequence format incorrect (Runtime error in 'SeqFact': Sequence not a factorization list).

rubrics_metrics.name: Working with factorization sequences safely (SeqFact, Facint, arithmetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: SeqFact builds a factorization sequence from [<prime, exponent>, ...]. Facint(Q) converts a factorization sequence Q to the corresponding integer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arithmetic: multiplying two factorization sequences merges exponents; division requires exact quotient; addition/subtraction of factorization sequences returns representation of sum/difference which is recomputed as a factorization sequence (operands must represent distinct integers for subtraction). Example: a := Factorization(...); b := Factorization(...); a * b yields combined factorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modular arithmetic intrinsics and recommended usage (Modexp, Modinv, Modsqrt, Solution, ChineseRemainderTheorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions for modular arithmetic: Modexp(a,k,n) returns a^k mod n efficiently (reducing intermediate powers), Modinv(a,n) returns inverse ab ≡ 1 (mod n) when gcd(a,n)=1, Modsqrt(a,n) returns b with b^2 ≡ a (mod n), Order(a,n) gives multiplicative order, IsPrimitive/PrimitiveRoot find primitive roots, Solution(A,B,N) solves systems of linear congruences (CRT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Modexp rather than a^k mod n when exponent k is large — Modexp reduces modulo n during powering and is far more efficient (timing example given). Solution(A,B,N) implements Chinese Remainder Theorem; moduli must be pairwise coprime. Example: Solution(8,7,11) returns 5 for 8x ≡ 7 (mod 11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue class rings construction and behavior (ResidueClassRing(n), quo, ideals in residue rings)
rubrics_metrics.description: ResidueClassRing(n) constructs ZZ/nZZ. For ZZ all subrings are ideals and are principal; quo<Z | I> and quo<Z | n> produce same residue class ring as ResidueClassRing(n). Ideals in residue class rings can be created via ideal< R | generators >.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating an ideal of ZZ by generators Magma returns a single generator (principal ideal). Parent of elements of an ideal of ZZ is ZZ itself rather than the ideal. Use Generator(I) to get generator; Set(I) lists elements when finite (e.g., ideal of Z6 generated by 2 has Set {0,2,4}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue class ring intrinsics (Modulus, Generator, AdditiveGroup, UnitGroup, PrimitiveElement, IsSquare, SquareRoot, AllSquareRoots, Solution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions for residue class rings: Modulus(R) returns the generator n for R = ZZ/nZZ. Generator(R) gives canonical generator of residue class ring. AdditiveGroup(R) and MultiplicativeGroup(R)/UnitGroup(R) return isomorphic groups and maps. PrimitiveElement(R) / PrimitiveRoot(R) returns an element generating the units if found. IsSquare, SquareRoot, AllSquareRoots handle squares. Solution(a,b) solves ax ≡ b (mod modulus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PrimitiveElement returns zero if no primitive element exists or cannot be found (zero chosen since zero is never primitive). Modulus(R) equals Modulus(I) for ideals I of R. Use these intrinsics when working with residues and solving congruences; examples provided (PrimitiveElement(Z38) -> 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Set(R) and iteration when ring is finite
rubrics_metrics.description: If Magma knows R is finite then the set of elements is Set(R) and it is possible to iterate over R (e.g., 'x in R' in a constructor or for-loop).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This depends on IsFinite(R) being true. Many algorithms/constructors rely on enumerating elements (e.g., computing additive/multiplicative groups) and will error or be infeasible if the ring is infinite or Magma doesn't know it is finite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories / naming conventions (RngInt, FldRat, RngIntRes, RngIntEltFact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Magma uses category names for types: the integer ring category is RngInt, rational field category FldRat, residue class rings and their ideals category RngIntRes, and factorization sequences category RngIntEltFact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing category names helps understand available intrinsics and type-checking behavior; examples in the text show Category(x) comparisons and Type($1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance/efficiency guidance (prefer modular intrinsics and reuse factorizations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specialized intrinsics that avoid large intermediate values (e.g., Modexp for modular exponentiation) and reuse factorization sequences as inputs to functions to avoid recomputing expensive factorizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: timing shows Modexp is orders of magnitude faster than naive exponentiation followed by mod for large exponents; passing Factorization(...) outputs directly to arithmetical functions avoids repeated factorization work. Where factorization is the dominant cost, many functions accept a factorization sequence as an argument.
